title: Optimal Betting Odds Against Insider Traders
key_finding: A bookmaker facing a share of insiders optimally widens margins and shades longshot odds, so the favourite-longshot bias arises as a defence against informed money.
relevance_to_system: Explains why a soft book's longshot prices are systematically too short, so naive de-vigged probabilities overstate longshot chances.

title: Measuring the Incidence of Insider Trading in a Market for State-Contingent Claims
key_finding: Fitting the insider model to UK horse-racing odds implies insider trading of roughly 2 percent of turnover and gives the basis of the Shin de-vig method.
relevance_to_system: Provides the Shin de-vig used to recover fair probabilities from a single book's odds.

title: Prices of State Contingent Claims with Insider Traders, and the Favourite-Longshot Bias
key_finding: Shows formally that insider presence produces bookmaker prices with a favourite-longshot bias and an overround increasing in the number of runners.
relevance_to_system: Shows that a book's margin is unevenly loaded across outcomes, so proportional de-vigging is biased.

title: Anomalies: Parimutuel Betting Markets: Racetracks and Lotteries
key_finding: Surveys evidence that favourites are underbet and longshots overbet in racetrack markets, with longshot returns far below the track take.
relevance_to_system: Establishes the baseline that betting markets are close to efficient apart from predictable biases that rarely exceed the margin.

title: The Favourite-Longshot Bias and Market Efficiency in UK Football Betting
authors: M. Cain; D. Law; D. Peel
key_finding: Finds a favourite-longshot bias in UK fixed-odds football correct-score and match-result markets, with longshot bets earning much lower returns.
relevance_to_system: Directly relevant because longshot in-play outcomes such as unlikely scorelines are where a soft book's margin is heaviest.

title: The Favourite-Longshot Bias, Bookmaker Margins and Insider Trading in a Variety of Betting Markets
authors: M. Cain; D. Law; D. Peel
key_finding: Applies the Shin model across horse racing, greyhounds and football and finds the bias and implied insider share vary by market.
relevance_to_system: Shows de-vig choice should be market-specific, not one formula for every in-play market.

title: Market Efficiency and the Favorite-Longshot Bias: The Baseball Betting Market
key_finding: Finds a reverse favourite-longshot bias in MLB money-line betting that is too small to yield profits after the margin.
relevance_to_system: Shows the direction of the bias is market-dependent and rarely exploitable, so it is no reliable edge source.

title: Explaining the Favorite-Long Shot Bias: Is it Risk-Love or Misperceptions?
key_finding: Using exotic-bet prices, argues probability misperception explains the racetrack favourite-longshot bias better than risk-loving preferences.
relevance_to_system: Shows that prices embed systematic probability distortions that a model must address explicitly rather than assume away.

title: The Favorite-Longshot Bias: An Overview of the Main Explanations
venue: Handbook of Sports and Lottery Markets
key_finding: Reviews risk-love, misperception, heterogeneous beliefs, private information and market-power explanations of the bias.
relevance_to_system: Frames why apparent model-versus-market gaps often reflect structural pricing rather than true edge.

title: Estimating Preferences under Risk: The Case of Racetrack Bettors
key_finding: Structural estimates on UK racing data favour cumulative prospect theory style preferences over expected utility to explain longshot pricing.
relevance_to_system: Implies market odds embed behavioural distortions that differ across the probability range, which affects calibration of de-vigged inputs.

title: Efficiency of the Market for Racetrack Betting
authors: D.B. Hausch; W.T. Ziemba; M. Rubinstein
key_finding: Win markets are close to efficient, but place and show pools sometimes misprice relative to win-implied probabilities, enabling a small Kelly-sized profit.
relevance_to_system: Precedent that only rare cross-market inconsistencies, not single-book model gaps, have produced documented positive returns.

title: Why is There a Favourite-Longshot Bias in British Racetrack Betting Markets
key_finding: Finds the bias is stronger in races with less public information, consistent with bookmakers protecting against insiders.
relevance_to_system: Live in-play markets with thin information are where bookmaker protective shading is likely largest.

title: Are Sports Bettors Biased toward Longshots, Favorites, or Both? A Literature Review
key_finding: Reviews the sports betting literature and finds the favourite-longshot bias is widespread but not universal, with reverse biases in some markets.
relevance_to_system: Supports treating bias corrections as empirical per-market estimates rather than fixed rules.

title: Risk aversion and favourite-longshot bias in a competitive fixed-odds betting market
key_finding: Shows a competitive fixed-odds bookmaker market with risk-averse bettors holding heterogeneous beliefs can generate the favourite-longshot bias, consistent with football odds data.
relevance_to_system: Shows the bias can persist even in competitive soft-book markets, so it is a structural feature to correct for.

title: Information, Prices and Efficiency in a Fixed-Odds Betting Market
key_finding: Tests UK fixed-odds football prices against expert tipster forecasts and finds no profitable strategy after the bookmaker margin.
relevance_to_system: Early evidence that public information is priced into football odds.

title: Information and efficiency: an empirical study of a fixed odds betting market
key_finding: Finds English football fixed odds deviate from efficiency in ways consistent with bookmakers exploiting bettor sentiment, with some strategies profitable in sample.
relevance_to_system: Shows soft-book prices can be deliberately biased toward bettor sentiment, which a de-vig cannot remove.

title: Modelling Association Football Scores and Inefficiencies in the Football Betting Market
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C
key_finding: A time-weighted Poisson model with a low-score correction yields positive returns only when betting where model-to-bookmaker probability ratios exceed a threshold.
relevance_to_system: Foundational for the system's Poisson approach and shows edge needed a high threshold, not any positive gap.

title: The value of statistical forecasts in the UK association football betting market
key_finding: Statistical model probabilities contain information beyond bookmaker odds in some segments, but exploitable mispricing is limited and inconsistent.
relevance_to_system: Shows model edges against bookmakers are small and segment-specific.

title: Forecasting football results and the efficiency of fixed-odds betting
key_finding: An ordered probit model using public information produces positive returns only in selective end-of-season matches.
relevance_to_system: Edges are narrow and context-dependent rather than broad model-versus-market gaps.

title: Odds-setters as forecasters: The case of English football
authors: D. Forrest; J. Goddard; R. Simmons
key_finding: Bookmaker odds became more efficient over 1998 to 2003, outperforming a benchmark statistical model by the end of the period.
relevance_to_system: Bookmaker odds tend to beat statistical models, so model-versus-market gaps are more often model error.

title: Sentiment in the betting market on Spanish football
key_finding: Bookmakers offered more generous odds on teams with large fan bases such as Barcelona and Real Madrid, consistent with sentiment-driven demand.
relevance_to_system: Soft-book prices contain demand-driven distortions that differ by team.

title: Sentimental Preferences and the Organizational Regime of Betting Markets
authors: E. Franck; E. Verbeek; S. Nüesch
key_finding: Bookmakers exploit sentiment toward popular teams while betting exchanges show less sentiment bias.
relevance_to_system: Exchange prices are a cleaner fair-value reference than a single soft bookmaker.

title: Prediction Accuracy of Different Market Structures: Bookmakers Versus a Betting Exchange
authors: E. Franck; E. Verbeek; S. Nüesch
venue: International Journal of Forecasting (SSRN version cited)
key_finding: Betfair exchange prices forecast European football results more accurately than bookmaker odds.
relevance_to_system: Supports using exchange or sharp odds as the benchmark against which to measure edge.

title: Online bookmakers' odds as forecasts: The case of European soccer leagues
key_finding: Bookmaker odds forecast accuracy improved over time, and books differ meaningfully in accuracy.
relevance_to_system: A single soft book may be among the less accurate, so its de-vigged odds are a weak anchor.

title: How Efficient is the European Football Betting Market? Evidence from Arbitrage and Trading Strategies
authors: N. Vlastakis; G. Dotsis; R.N. Markellos
key_finding: Cross-bookmaker arbitrage opportunities exist but are rare, and simple model strategies earn little after margins.
relevance_to_system: Profitable opportunities came from price dispersion across books, not from one book against a model.

title: Profiting from arbitrage and odds biases of the European football gambling market
venue: The Journal of Gambling Business and Economics
key_finding: Arbitrage across many bookmakers was available but declined over time, and longshot biases persisted.
relevance_to_system: Line shopping across books is a more plausible edge than single-book model gaps.

title: Are betting markets efficient? Evidence from European Football Championships
key_finding: Finds a reverse longshot pattern where betting heavy favourites earned positive returns in some European competitions.
relevance_to_system: Bias direction varies by competition, so fixed bias corrections are risky.

title: Efficiency of Online Football Betting Markets
venue: International Journal of Forecasting (SSRN version cited)
key_finding: Across 41 bookmakers and 11 European leagues, most markets are efficient, with inefficiencies in only a few leagues.
relevance_to_system: Persistent pre-match edges are rare and league-specific.

title: Bookmakers' mispricing of the disappeared home advantage in the German Bundesliga after the COVID-19 break
authors: D. Winkelmann; C. Deutscher; M. Ötting
key_finding: Bookmakers were slow to price the loss of home advantage in empty-stadium matches, allowing temporary profits on away teams.
relevance_to_system: Genuine soft-book edges arise from structural shocks and are short-lived.

title: Are Sports Betting Markets Semi-Strong Efficient? Evidence From the COVID-19 Pandemic
authors: P.F. Meier; R. Flepp; E. Franck
key_finding: Markets adapted quickly to the home-advantage shock, with only short-lived inefficiencies.
relevance_to_system: Any edge from a regime change disappears quickly, so a persistent edge claim needs strong evidence.

title: Why do some soccer bettors lose more money than others?
authors: R. Buhagiar; D. Cortis; P.W.S. Newall
venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance
key_finding: Bets on longer odds and on complex markets lose substantially more than bets on favourites because of higher embedded margins.
relevance_to_system: Exotic in-play markets carry larger margins, raising the edge bar.

title: Anyone for Tennis (Betting)?
key_finding: Finds a favourite-longshot bias in tennis betting prices, with longshots overpriced.
relevance_to_system: Shows the bias is general across sports and must be modelled in de-vigging.

title: What Causes the Favorite-Longshot Bias? Further Evidence from Tennis
key_finding: The bias is stronger in lower-profile tennis matches, consistent with an insider-protection explanation.
relevance_to_system: Lower-profile matches carry larger bookmaker shading, which inflates false edges.

title: On determining probability forecasts from betting odds
key_finding: Shin-model probabilities are more accurate than basic normalisation or regression-based methods across bookmakers and leagues.
relevance_to_system: The system should use Shin or similar rather than proportional de-vigging.

title: Adjusting Bookmaker's Odds to Allow for Overround
authors: S. Clarke; S. Kovalchik; M. Ingram
key_finding: Compares multiplicative, additive, Shin and power methods and finds the power and Shin methods fit the longshot bias better than proportional scaling.
relevance_to_system: De-vig choice changes fair-probability estimates enough to create or erase apparent edges.

title: Beating the market with a bad predictive model
key_finding: Shows profitability depends on a model's errors being decorrelated from the market's, not on accuracy alone.
relevance_to_system: Edge requires information the market lacks, not just a model that differs from the market.

title: Exploiting sports-betting market using machine learning
authors: O. Hubáček; G. Šourek; F. Železný
key_finding: Decorrelating model predictions from bookmaker odds improved returns in NBA betting experiments.
relevance_to_system: Supports evaluating whether model gaps reflect independent information.

title: Market Efficiency in Person-to-Person Betting
authors: M.A. Smith; D. Paton; L. Vaughan Williams
key_finding: Betting exchange prices show a smaller favourite-longshot bias than bookmaker odds in UK horse racing.
relevance_to_system: Exchange prices are a better fair-value benchmark than soft-book odds.

title: Information and Efficiency: Goal Arrival in Soccer Betting
key_finding: Betfair prices update to goals scored just before half-time quickly and fully, with no exploitable drift during the break.
relevance_to_system: In-play exchange prices are efficient after goals, so post-goal model gaps against a book are unlikely to be real edge.

title: The role of surprise: Understanding overreaction and underreaction to unanticipated events using in-play soccer betting market
venue: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
key_finding: In Betfair in-play football markets prices generally underreact to goals but overreact when the goal is highly surprising, such as an underdog scoring.
relevance_to_system: Post-goal mispricing depends on how surprising the goal is, so a uniform post-goal model gap is not a reliable edge signal.

title: Informational efficiency and behaviour within in-play prediction markets
authors: G. Angelini; L. De Angelis; C. Singleton
key_finding: Using the first goal in Betfair football markets as clean news, finds pre-match and in-play mispricing explained by a reverse favourite-longshot bias, largest after surprising late goals by longshot teams whose win chances the market underestimates.
relevance_to_system: Even exchange in-play prices carry state-dependent bias after goals, so any post-goal edge must be measured against exchange prices and is concentrated in specific surprise states.

title: A birth process model for association football matches
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series D
key_finding: Scoring rates rise over a match and depend on the current score, so a constant-rate Poisson is misspecified for in-play pricing.
relevance_to_system: The system's remaining-goals Poisson needs time and score-state dependent rates.

title: Testing the Efficiency of Markets in the 2002 World Cup
key_finding: Intrade prices responded quickly to goals but continued drifting afterwards, leaving small but untradeable inefficiencies.
relevance_to_system: In-play gaps after goals are small and tend to fall below trading costs.

title: Evidence of In-Play Insider Trading on a U.K. Betting Exchange
key_finding: Exchange prices in tennis moved before televised events, indicating some traders had faster information.
relevance_to_system: Latency risk works against a bettor relying on delayed feeds, which can turn apparent edges into adverse selection.

title: Why are Gambling Markets Organised so Differently from Financial Markets?
key_finding: Bookmakers do not balance their books and instead set prices to exploit bettor biases, which works because they are better forecasters.
relevance_to_system: Soft-book prices are deliberately biased and a book wins by limiting skilled bettors.

title: Beating the bookies with their own numbers - and how the online sports betting market is rigged
authors: L. Kaunitz; S. Zhong; J. Kreiner
key_finding: Betting where a book's odds exceeded the consensus-implied fair price was profitable in simulation and live trading until bookmakers restricted their accounts.
relevance_to_system: The documented edge came from consensus pricing against stale soft odds, and winners get limited.

title: Inter-market Arbitrage in Betting
authors: E. Franck; E. Verbeek; S. Nüesch
key_finding: Combining bookmaker and exchange prices produced frequent arbitrage opportunities in European football.
relevance_to_system: Exchange prices are an essential reference, and soft-book value is identifiable against them.

title: Betting Exchanges: The Future of Sports Betting?
key_finding: Exchanges offer better prices than bookmakers for most outcomes, especially longshots.
relevance_to_system: Supports benchmarking edge against exchange prices rather than a single soft book.

title: NFL bettor biases and price setting: further tests of the Levitt hypothesis of sportsbook behaviour
key_finding: Betting volumes are unbalanced toward favourites and overs, consistent with sportsbooks shading prices against public biases.
relevance_to_system: A soft book's price shading leads model gaps to cluster on outcomes that books have shaded.

title: Does Sportsbook.com Set Pointspreads to Maximize Profits?
key_finding: Uses sportsbook bet-share data to show books accept unbalanced action consistent with profit-maximising price setting.
relevance_to_system: Shows soft-book prices are strategic, not neutral probability estimates.

title: Sports forecasting: a comparison of the forecast accuracy of prediction markets, betting odds and tipsters
key_finding: Betting odds and prediction markets forecast German football similarly well and both beat tipsters, but neither leads to a profitable strategy after margins.
relevance_to_system: Market odds are hard to beat with public information.

title: A New Interpretation of Information Rate
key_finding: Maximising expected log wealth gives the optimal growth rate, with stake fraction set by edge divided by odds.
relevance_to_system: Kelly is only optimal when the true probabilities are known, so model error becomes overbetting.

title: The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market
venue: Handbook of Asset and Liability Management
key_finding: Overbetting past twice the Kelly fraction yields negative growth, and fractional Kelly trades growth for much lower drawdowns.
relevance_to_system: An overestimated edge pushes full Kelly toward the negative-growth region.

title: Growth Versus Security in Dynamic Investment Analysis
authors: L.C. MacLean; W.T. Ziemba; G. Blazenko
key_finding: Fractional Kelly strategies trade expected growth for higher probability of reaching wealth goals and avoiding drawdowns.
relevance_to_system: Supports fractional Kelly with explicit drawdown targets.

title: Optimal Betting Under Parameter Uncertainty: Improving the Kelly Criterion
key_finding: When probabilities are estimated, shrinking the Kelly stake improves expected log growth, and the shrinkage needed rises with estimation uncertainty.
relevance_to_system: The system should shrink stakes in proportion to model uncertainty.

title: Risk-Constrained Kelly Gambling
authors: E. Busseti; E.K. Ryu; S. Boyd
key_finding: Formulates Kelly with a drawdown-probability constraint as a convex problem, giving stakes with bounded drawdown at modest growth cost.
relevance_to_system: Provides a principled replacement for ad hoc Kelly fractions.

title: Optimal sports betting strategies in practice: an experimental review
authors: M. Uhrín; G. Šourek; O. Hubáček; F. Železný
key_finding: Across horse racing, basketball and football, full Kelly is often ruinous in practice, while fractional or risk-constrained Kelly is more robust.
relevance_to_system: Supports strict fractional Kelly and drawdown caps.

title: Portfolio choice and the Bayesian Kelly criterion
key_finding: Derives Kelly-type betting when probabilities are learned over time, giving smaller stakes under uncertainty.
relevance_to_system: The edge estimate should be treated as uncertain and updated, not plugged in as known.

title: Why we should not make mean log of wealth big though years to act are long
key_finding: Argues that maximising log wealth is not optimal for every utility and does not eliminate the risk of large losses.
relevance_to_system: Reminds that Kelly sizing still allows large drawdowns.

title: Algorithms for Optimal Allocation of Bets on Many Simultaneous Events
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C
key_finding: Gives algorithms for Kelly allocation across many simultaneous bets and shows naive independent sizing overbets.
relevance_to_system: Concurrent in-play bets need joint sizing, not independent Kelly per bet.

title: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
key_finding: Defines strictly proper scoring rules such as log score, Brier and CRPS that reward honest probabilistic forecasts.
relevance_to_system: Models should be evaluated with proper scoring rules rather than hit rate or short-run ROI.

title: Solving the Problem of Inadequate Scoring Rules for Assessing Probabilistic Football Forecast Models
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports
key_finding: Argues the ranked probability score suits ordered home-draw-away football outcomes better than unordered scores.
relevance_to_system: Provides a score for the system's match-result forecasts.

title: Are betting returns a useful measure of accuracy in (sports) forecasting?
key_finding: Betting returns are noisy and can rank models differently from proper scores, so they need large samples to be informative.
relevance_to_system: Short-run ROI cannot validate the model; proper scores and closing-line value are needed.

title: A Scoring System for Probability Forecasts of Ranked Categories
key_finding: Introduces the ranked probability score for ordered categorical forecasts.
relevance_to_system: Source of the RPS used to score football outcome forecasts.

title: Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability
key_finding: Introduces the Brier score as mean squared error of probability forecasts.
relevance_to_system: Baseline proper score for the system's binary in-play markets.

title: Machine Learning for Sports Betting: Should Model Selection Be Based on Accuracy or Calibration?
venue: Machine Learning with Applications (SSRN version DOI cited)
key_finding: On NBA betting data, selecting models by calibration rather than accuracy produced substantially higher and positive betting returns, while accuracy-selected models lost money.
relevance_to_system: Calibration of model probabilities matters more than accuracy for Kelly-sized betting.

title: Evaluating probabilistic forecasts of football matches: the case against the ranked probability score
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports
key_finding: Shows the ranked probability score can favour less skilful forecasts and recommends the ignorance (log) score.
relevance_to_system: Suggests log loss as the primary metric for the in-play model.

title: Comparing Predictive Accuracy
venue: Journal of Business and Economic Statistics
key_finding: Provides a test of whether two forecasts differ significantly in expected loss.
relevance_to_system: The system should test model-versus-market score differences statistically.

title: The Betting Odds Rating System: Using soccer forecasts to forecast soccer
key_finding: Ratings derived from betting odds forecast football outcomes better than Elo-type ratings based on results.
relevance_to_system: Market odds are strong forecasts and a hard benchmark for a Poisson model.

title: Using ELO ratings for match result prediction in association football
key_finding: Elo-based models predicted results reasonably but were outperformed by bookmaker odds and did not yield profits.
relevance_to_system: Statistical models are generally inferior to market odds.
